content: The document titled Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission of Hepatitis B Virus: Guidelines on Antiviral Prophylaxis in Pregnancy (July 2020) provides a detailed analysis of the impact and cost-effectiveness of implementing peripartum antiviral therapy to reduce the transmission of hepatitis B virus (HBV) from mothers to their newborns. The analysis was conducted by a team of experts from Imperial College London, the Pasteur Institute in Paris, and the World Health Organization (WHO). Background Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a significant global health burden. The WHO's 2016 Global Health Sector Strategy (GHSS) on viral hepatitis set a target to reduce new HBV infections by 90% by 2030. Currently, the primary WHO recommendation for preventing mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HBV is the administration of a birth dose (BD) of the HBV vaccine within 24 hours of birth. However, emerging evidence suggests that adding peripartum antiviral therapy (PPT) could further reduce HBV transmission rates. As a result, the WHO Guidelines Development Group (GDG) is reviewing the evidence for incorporating PPT into PMTCT strategies. Methods A dynamic, age-, sex-, and region-structured simulation model of the global HBV epidemic was adapted to evaluate the regional impact and cost-effectiveness of scaling up PPT for pregnant women. The model incorporates data on HBV surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg) prevalence, liver cancer deaths, national demographic data, and intervention coverage levels for infant and BD vaccination. Transmission pathways include mother-to-child, child-to-child, and population-wide transmission, with the relative strengths of these pathways inferred through calibration. Strategies Evaluated Four main strategies were assessed: 1. Strategy 1 (Status Quo SQ): Infant vaccination coverage scaled up to 90% (or maintained at higher levels if already achieved). 2. Strategy 2: Infant vaccination and timely BD vaccination scaled up to 90%. 3. Strategy 3: PPT guided by HBV viral load testing. Pregnant women testing positive for HBsAg undergo viral load testing, and those with high viral loads (≥200,000 IU/mL) are treated with tenofovir. 4. Strategy 4: PPT guided by HBeAg testing. Pregnant women testing positive for HBsAg undergo HBeAg testing, and those testing positive for HBeAg are treated with tenofovir. PPT interventions were modeled to include up to four months of antiviral therapy and monitoring, starting in 2021. The analysis assumed that PPT would be incremental to BD vaccination without the use of hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG), which is not universally recommended by WHO due to cost and logistical challenges. Economic Analysis The economic analysis was conducted from a health provider perspective, with costs and health outcomes discounted at 3% over a long-term horizon (to 2100). Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) were calculated relative to two baselines: (1) the status quo (SQ) and (2) BD vaccination coverage at 90%. Costs included diagnostic tests (HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV viral load), antiviral therapy, and treatment monitoring. The analysis also explored the impact of varying costs, including the management of end-stage liver disease (ESLD), on cost-effectiveness. Results Impact Scaling up BD vaccination to 90% coverage has the largest incremental impact in reducing new infections and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) in regions where BD coverage is currently low. Globally, this strategy could avert 14 million new neonatal HBV infections and 38,500 DALYs over the next 10 years. Over the long term (to 2100), it could prevent 40 million new infections and 122 million DALYs. Adding PPT to BD vaccination could avert an additional 3–7 million neonatal infections and 22–25 million DALYs globally by 2100. Cost-Effectiveness Scaling up BD vaccination is the most cost-effective strategy in most regions, with ICERs ranging from $133 to $952 per DALY averted. In eight world regions, ICERs are below $300 per DALY averted. PPT strategies guided by HBV viral load (Strategy 3) or HBeAg testing (Strategy 4) are less cost-effective than BD vaccination alone but may still be cost-effective in certain regions. ICERs for PPT strategies vary widely between regions, ranging from $890 to $7,355 per DALY averted. The cost-effectiveness of PPT strategies depends heavily on the relative costs of diagnostic tests. In most regions, the difference in ICERs between viral load-guided and HBeAg-guided strategies is less than $200. Regional Analysis In the South-East Asian region, PPT strategies have ICERs of $2,214 (viral load-guided) and $2,319 (HBeAg-guided) per DALY averted. These ICERs are consistent with estimated health opportunity costs in only three of the 11 countries in the region, suggesting that PPT may not be cost-effective in the remaining countries unless diagnostic costs are reduced. If diagnostic costs were lowered, ICERs for PPT strategies in this region could decrease to $639–$672 per DALY averted, making them more cost-effective. Sensitivity Analysis The analysis explored the impact of varying assumptions about transmission parameters, the inclusion of HBIG, discount rates, and time horizons. Lowering the efficacy of BD and PPT strategies or increasing the costs of diagnostics significantly affected cost-effectiveness. Including the costs averted from managing ESLD (e.g., decompensated cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma) reduced ICERs, making PPT strategies more cost-effective in some regions. Conclusion Scaling up BD vaccination remains the most cost-effective strategy for preventing mother-to-child transmission of HBV in most regions. Adding PPT guided by either HBV viral load or HBeAg testing can further reduce HBV transmission but is less cost-effective and highly dependent on diagnostic costs. Reducing the costs of diagnostics and antiviral therapy could improve the cost-effectiveness of PPT strategies, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Further research is needed to refine cost estimates and assess the feasibility of implementing PPT at scale.
